claim: Reversible lysine acetylation plays essential roles in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: Reversible lysine acetylation is one of the most important protein posttranslational modifications that plays essential roles in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: Only a few lysine deacetylases (KDACs) have been identified in prokaryotes.
source: However, only a few lysine deacetylases (KDACs) have been identified in prokaryotes, perhaps in part due to their limited sequence homology.
evidence: This is presented as background knowledge about the state of the field.

claim: YcgC is a serine hydrolase involving Ser200 as the catalytic nucleophile for lysine deacetylation.
source: In-depth biochemical characterization confirmed that YcgC is a serine hydrolase involving Ser200 as the catalytic nucleophile for lysine deacetylation and does not use NAD+ or Zn2+ like other established KDACs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including mutagenesis studies and AEBSF labeling experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: YcgC does not use NAD+ or Zn2+ as cofactors.
source: In-depth biochemical characterization confirmed that YcgC is a serine hydrolase involving Ser200 as the catalytic nucleophile for lysine deacetylation and does not use NAD+ or Zn2+ like other established KDACs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing deacetylation activity in the absence of NAD+ and Zn2+, confirmed by HPLC and ICP-MS analyses.

claim: YcgC regulates transcription by catalyzing deacetylation of Lys52 and Lys62 of RutR.
source: Further, in vivo characterization demonstrated that YcgC regulates transcription by catalyzing deacetylation of Lys52 and Lys62 of a transcriptional repressor RutR.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data identifying these sites and qPCR data showing changes in gene expression.

claim: YcgC targets a distinct set of substrates from CobB.
source: Importantly, YcgC targets a distinct set of substrates from the only known E. coli KDAC CobB.
evidence: This is supported by global gene expression analysis and Western blot data showing different acetylation profiles.

claim: YcgC's bacterial homologs exhibit KDAC activity.
source: Analysis of YcgC's bacterial homologs confirmed that they also exhibit KDAC activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in acetylation profiles upon overexpression of homologs from different bacterial species.

claim: YcgC represents a novel family of prokaryotic KDACs.
source: YcgC thus represents a novel family of prokaryotic KDACs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of data showing unique mechanism, distinct substrates, and conserved activity among homologs.

claim: Many proteins are acetylated in Escherichia coli.
source: Recent mass spectrometry (MS) efforts have revealed that many proteins are acetylated in Escherichia coli, although only a single E. coli lysine deacetylase (KDAC), CobB, has been identified so far (Choudhary et al., 2009; Henriksen et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mass spectrometry studies.

claim: CobB is the only known E. coli KDAC prior to this study.
source: Recent mass spectrometry (MS) efforts have revealed that many proteins are acetylated in Escherichia coli, although only a single E. coli lysine deacetylase (KDAC), CobB, has been identified so far (Choudhary et al., 2009; Henriksen et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Induction of CobB has limited impact on reducing global protein acetylation levels.
source: The fact that induction of CobB only had a limited impact on reducing the global protein acetylation level suggests that additional KDACs may exist.
evidence: This is presented as an observation that motivates the search for additional KDACs.

claim: Additional KDACs may exist in E. coli beyond CobB.
source: The fact that induction of CobB only had a limited impact on reducing the global protein acetylation level suggests that additional KDACs may exist.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the limited effect of CobB induction.

claim: Homolog searching has failed to reveal additional KDACs in E. coli.
source: However, homolog searching has failed to reveal any additional KDACs in E. coli, presumably because these enzymes emerged via convergent evolution.
evidence: This is presented as a known limitation of bioinformatics approaches.

claim: KDACs may have emerged via convergent evolution.
source: However, homolog searching has failed to reveal any additional KDACs in E. coli, presumably because these enzymes emerged via convergent evolution.
evidence: This is speculation to explain why homology searches failed.

claim: Biochemical approaches have proven effective for identifying new enzymes resulting from convergent evolution.
source: In contrast to bioinformatics methods, biochemical approaches have proven effective for identifying new enzymes resulting from convergent evolution (Tsukada et al., 2006; Yamane et al., 2006), though their laborious, time-consuming nature has limited their applications to high-throughput, proteome-wide screens.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The clip-chip approach enables proteome-wide, activity-based search for novel KDACs.
source: Herein, we established a 'clip-chip' approach to enable a proteome-wide, activity-based search for novel KDACs in E. coli.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental results showing identification of YcgC using this method.

claim: The clip-chip strategy delivers thousands of purified proteins to a substrate of interest for parallel biochemical reactions.
source: The principle behind the clip-chip approach is the delivery of thousands of purified proteins spotted on a glass slide (e.g., a proteome microarray) to a substrate of interest immobilized on another slide (i.e., the substrate slide) such that thousands of desired biochemical reactions can be carried out in parallel, in order to identify new enzymes of interest (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is described in the methods and illustrated in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Protein droplets are immediately absorbed and kept locally in nitrocellulose, preventing cross-contamination.
source: Owing to the highly porous nature of nitrocellulose and the tiny volume of the protein droplets (0.3–0.5 nL), the delivered protein droplets are immediately absorbed and kept locally in the nitrocellulose, preventing cross-contamination.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of nitrocellulose and the experimental design.

claim: NhoA, RutR, and YceC have high endogenous acetylation levels.
source: To screen for new KDAC candidates in the E. coli proteome, we prepared separate substrate slides for three E. coli proteins, namely NhoA, RutR, and YceC, which were chosen because they have a rather high endogenous acetylation level and because CobB exhibits only modest ability to deacetylate them (Zhang et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CobB exhibits only modest ability to deacetylate NhoA, RutR, and YceC.
source: To screen for new KDAC candidates in the E. coli proteome, we prepared separate substrate slides for three E. coli proteins, namely NhoA, RutR, and YceC, which were chosen because they have a rather high endogenous acetylation level and because CobB exhibits only modest ability to deacetylate them (Zhang et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: 4256 individually purified E. coli proteins were used in the clip-chip screen.
source: After 4256 individually purified E. coli proteins (Chen et al., 2008) were spotted on plain glass slides, they were clipped separately onto the three substrate slides, followed by incubation with a standard deacetylase reaction buffer containing NAD+.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design with citation to the protein source.

claim: Four candidates showed significant deacetylation activities against at least one of the three substrates tested.
source: We identified four candidates that showed significant deacetylation activities against at least one of the three substrates tested.
evidence: This is based on the clip-chip screening results.

claim: YcgC can readily deacetylate RutR in vitro.
source: By evaluating the decrease in acetylation signals using an immunoblot assay with α-AcK, we confirmed that one of the candidates, YcgC, could readily deacetylate RutR in vitro, and that CobB also deacetylated RutR.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: CobB deacetylates RutR in vitro.
source: By evaluating the decrease in acetylation signals using an immunoblot assay with α-AcK, we confirmed that one of the candidates, YcgC, could readily deacetylate RutR in vitro, and that CobB also deacetylated RutR.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: YjgD did not show detectable deacetylation activity against RutR.
source: YjgD did not show any detectable deacetylation activity against RutR, while Gnd and YhbL showed slight activity (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Gnd and YhbL showed slight deacetylation activity against RutR.
source: YjgD did not show any detectable deacetylation activity against RutR, while Gnd and YhbL showed slight activity (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: YcgC showed KDAC activity against NhoA and YceC.
source: As YcgC also showed KDAC activity against NhoA and YceC (data not shown), we then focused on characterizing the function of YcgC.
evidence: This is stated as experimental observation though data is not shown.

claim: YcgC is previously known as DhaM, a subunit of dihydroacetone kinase complex.
source: YcgC is previously known as DhaM, a subunit of dihydroacetone kinase complex and a nonessential gene in E. coli.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about YcgC.

claim: YcgC is a nonessential gene in E. coli.
source: YcgC is previously known as DhaM, a subunit of dihydroacetone kinase complex and a nonessential gene in E. coli.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about YcgC.

claim: The endogenous level of YcgC is very low.
source: Because the endogenous level of YcgC is very low, YcgC was overexpressed on the wild-type background in the subsequent experiments.
evidence: This is an observation that motivated the experimental approach.

claim: The possibility that YcgC has intrinsic enzymatic activity has not been reported previously.
source: As the M subunit of the dihydroxyacetone kinase complex, the possibility that YcgC has intrinsic enzymatic activity has not been reported previously (Molin et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Class III deacetylases require NAD+ as a cofactor.
source: Therefore, we first determined whether YcgC also requires NAD+ and/or Zn2+ to deacetylate RutR, as class III deacetylases require NAD+ as a cofactor and other classes are dependent on Zn2+ (Thiagalingam et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Other classes of deacetylases are dependent on Zn2+.
source: Therefore, we first determined whether YcgC also requires NAD+ and/or Zn2+ to deacetylate RutR, as class III deacetylases require NAD+ as a cofactor and other classes are dependent on Zn2+ (Thiagalingam et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Endogenous RutR proteins are highly acetylated.
source: We chose RutR as the substrate for YcgC, because endogenous RutR proteins are highly acetylated and because it is known to regulate genes directly or indirectly involved in the complex pathways of pyrimidine and purine metabolism (Shimada et al., 2007; Shimada et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation and cited literature.

claim: RutR regulates genes directly or indirectly involved in pyrimidine and purine metabolism pathways.
source: We chose RutR as the substrate for YcgC, because endogenous RutR proteins are highly acetylated and because it is known to regulate genes directly or indirectly involved in the complex pathways of pyrimidine and purine metabolism (Shimada et al., 2007; Shimada et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: YcgC can deacetylate RutR effectively without NAD+ or Zn2+.
source: Immunoblotting of the deacetylation reactions clearly showed that YcgC could deacetylate RutR effectively, but this activity did not appear to be dependent on NAD+ or Zn2+ (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no detectable NAD+ in the YcgC-RutR reaction.
source: High-performance liquid chromatography analysis and inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), respectively, confirmed that there was no detectable NAD+ or Zn2+ in the reaction (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on HPLC analysis.

claim: There was no detectable Zn2+ in the YcgC-RutR reaction.
source: High-performance liquid chromatography analysis and inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), respectively, confirmed that there was no detectable NAD+ or Zn2+ in the reaction (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on ICP-MS analysis.

claim: Deacetylated RutR protein appears at a slightly lower molecular weight than acetylated RutR on Coomassie staining.
source: Of note, Coomassie staining of the decaetylated RutR protein product band appeared at a slightly lower molecular weight than acetylated RutR and this is explored below.
evidence: This is an observation from Coomassie staining experiments.

claim: Lys52 is an acetylated site in RutR protein.
source: We found that Lys52 and Lys62, present in the peptide sequences LEQIAELAGVSK52TNLLYYFPSK and TNLLYYFPSK62EALYIAVLR, respectively, were acetylated in RutR expressed in wild-type (WT) cells (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Lys62 is an acetylated site in RutR protein.
source: We found that Lys52 and Lys62, present in the peptide sequences LEQIAELAGVSK52TNLLYYFPSK and TNLLYYFPSK62EALYIAVLR, respectively, were acetylated in RutR expressed in wild-type (WT) cells (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: After RutR was incubated with YcgC, acetylation of K52 was no longer detectable.
source: However, after RutR was incubated with YcgC, acetylation of K52 or K62 was no longer detectable (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: After RutR was incubated with YcgC, acetylation of K62 was no longer detectable.
source: However, after RutR was incubated with YcgC, acetylation of K52 or K62 was no longer detectable (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: YcgC effectively deacetylates RutR on residues K52 and K62 in vitro.
source: Therefore, YcgC effectively deacetylates RutR on residues K52 and K62 in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the LC-MS/MS data.

claim: Acetylation levels of RutR proteins were significantly reduced in a YcgC expression level-dependent manner.
source: Using IP-coupled immunoblotting analysis, we observed that acetylation levels of RutR proteins were significantly reduced in a YcgC expression level-dependent manner as detected by a custom-made α-YcgC monoclonal antibody (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by IP-coupled immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The total amount of RutR was not affected by YcgC induction.
source: In contrast, the total amount of RutR was not affected by YcgC induction (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: YcgC effectively deacetylates RutR in vivo without affecting its stability.
source: These results confirmed that YcgC effectively deacetylates RutR in vivo without affecting its stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the IP-coupled immunoblotting data.

claim: Mutation of either K52 or K62 resulted in a substantial loss of acetylation signals in RutR.
source: After transformation of these mutants into E. coli, subsequent IP-coupled immunoblotting demonstrated that, compared with WT RutR, mutation of either K52 or K62 resulted in a substantial loss of acetylation signals in RutR, with the K52/62Q double mutant showing the lowest acetylation signals (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by IP-coupled immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The K52/62Q double mutant showed the lowest acetylation signals.
source: After transformation of these mutants into E. coli, subsequent IP-coupled immunoblotting demonstrated that, compared with WT RutR, mutation of either K52 or K62 resulted in a substantial loss of acetylation signals in RutR, with the K52/62Q double mutant showing the lowest acetylation signals (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by IP-coupled immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Both K52 and K62 are major acetylation sites in RutR.
source: These results suggest that both K52 and K62 are major acetylation sites in RutR, and can be effectively deacetylated by YcgC in E. coli.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: K52 and K62 can be effectively deacetylated by YcgC in E. coli.
source: These results suggest that both K52 and K62 are major acetylation sites in RutR, and can be effectively deacetylated by YcgC in E. coli.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis and in vivo deacetylation data.

claim: Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail could significantly inhibit YcgC's deacetylase activity.
source: We found that Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (with or without ethylene glycol tetraacetic acid [EGTA]; Thermo Scientific, Rockford, IL) and Complete Protease Tablet (Roche, Mannheim, Germany) could significantly inhibit YcgC's deacetylase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Complete Protease Tablet could significantly inhibit YcgC's deacetylase activity.
source: We found that Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (with or without ethylene glycol tetraacetic acid [EGTA]; Thermo Scientific, Rockford, IL) and Complete Protease Tablet (Roche, Mannheim, Germany) could significantly inhibit YcgC's deacetylase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The active component in the Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail was AEBSF.
source: Further analysis revealed that the active component in the Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail was a serine hydrolase inhibitor 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonyl fluoride (AEBSF), but not the other components.
evidence: This is supported by testing individual components of the inhibitor cocktail.

claim: YcgC's deacetylase activity could not be inhibited by trichostatin A, SAHA, and NAM.
source: Additional assays demonstrated that YcgC's deacetylase activity could not be inhibited by well-known deacetylase inhibitors, including trichostatin A, SAHA (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid), and NAM (Nicotinamide), and that hydrolase inhibitors, phenylmethylsulfonyl (PMSF), leupeptin, ethylenediaminetetracetic acid and EGTA, showed no detectable inhibition of YcgC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: PMSF, leupeptin, EDTA and EGTA showed no detectable inhibition of YcgC.
source: Additional assays demonstrated that YcgC's deacetylase activity could not be inhibited by well-known deacetylase inhibitors, including trichostatin A, SAHA (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid), and NAM (Nicotinamide), and that hydrolase inhibitors, phenylmethylsulfonyl (PMSF), leupeptin, ethylenediaminetetracetic acid and EGTA, showed no detectable inhibition of YcgC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: YcgC likely belongs to the serine hydrolase family.
source: Thus, it is likely that YcgC belongs to the serine hydrolase family, which has no significant homology to any of the annotated KDACs to date.
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibitor studies showing AEBSF inhibition.

claim: The serine hydrolase family has no significant homology to any of the annotated KDACs to date.
source: Thus, it is likely that YcgC belongs to the serine hydrolase family, which has no significant homology to any of the annotated KDACs to date.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of protein families.

claim: Five Ser residues (S7, S10, S73, S77, and S200) are highly conserved among YcgC's prokaryotic homologs.
source: To identify which Ser residue in YcgC was most critical for its hydrolase (KDAC) activity, we examined five Ser residues, namely S7, S10, S73, S77, and S200, which are highly conserved among its prokaryotic homologs on the basis of protein sequence alignment.
evidence: This is based on protein sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The 5SA mutant of YcgC appeared devoid of RutR deacetylase activity.
source: Next, we created a quintuple Ser-to-Ala mutant (i.e., 5SA) in YcgC and tested its ability to deacetylate RutR in vitro. As compared with the WT YcgC, the 5SA mutant appeared devoid of RutR deacetylase activity (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Ser200 was the only conserved residue that was covalently labeled with AEBSF.
source: To determine which of the five Ser residues was likely to be the catalytic nucleophile for hydrolase activity, we incubated WT YcgC with hydrolase inhibitor AEBSF and the following MS/MS analysis revealed that Ser200 was the only conserved residue that was covalently labeled with AEBSF (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The S200A mutant of YcgC showed no detectable deacetylase activity.
source: To confirm its importance, a Ser200-to-Ala (S200A) mutant was created and tested in the same in vitro assay. As anticipated, the deacetylase activity was not detectable with S200A YcgC, establishing Ser200 as the likely key catalytic residue.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Ser200 is the likely key catalytic residue of YcgC.
source: To confirm its importance, a Ser200-to-Ala (S200A) mutant was created and tested in the same in vitro assay. As anticipated, the deacetylase activity was not detectable with S200A YcgC, establishing Ser200 as the likely key catalytic residue.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis and AEBSF labeling data.

claim: RutR deacetylation by YcgC reproducibly induces faster migration on SDS-PAGE.
source: As mentioned, RutR deacetylation by YcgC reproducibly induces faster migration on sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE).
evidence: This is an observation from multiple experiments.

claim: RutR deacetylation by CobB induces faster migration on SDS-PAGE.
source: This behavior was also observed with deacetylation by the sirtuin family member CobB (Figure 2a; Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 3a.

claim: N-terminal Edman sequencing of RutR after YcgC treatment showed N-terminal truncation with loss of 14 or 11 residues.
source: N-terminal Edman sequencing of RutR after YcgC treatment showed N-terminal truncation with loss of 14 residues (N-MTQGAVKTTGKRSR) or 11 residues (N-MTQGAVKTTGK).
evidence: This is based on N-terminal Edman sequencing data.

claim: RutR without YcgC treatment showed no N-terminal truncation.
source: RutR without YcgC treatment was also sequenced, no N-terminal truncation was observed.
evidence: This is based on N-terminal Edman sequencing data.

claim: Treatment of RutR with CobB induces N-terminal truncation with loss of 14 residues.
source: However, we believe this is unlikely since treatment of RutR with the sirtuin CobB, mechanistically and structurally unrelated to YcgC, induces a similar N-terminal truncation in RutR, visualized by SDS-PAGE and detected by N-terminal sequencing with loss of 14 residues.
evidence: This is based on N-terminal sequencing data.

claim: N-terminal cleavage of RutR results from autoproteolysis.
source: We suspect that this N-terminal cleavage of RutR results from autoproteolysis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that both YcgC and CobB induce similar cleavage.

claim: Heat-denatured RutR could be partially deacetylated by both YcgC and CobB.
source: As shown in Figure 3, heat-denatured RutR could be partially deacetylated by both YcgC and CobB, but did not show a downshifting on SDS-PAGE.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Heat-denatured RutR did not show downshifting on SDS-PAGE after deacetylation.
source: As shown in Figure 3, heat-denatured RutR could be partially deacetylated by both YcgC and CobB, but did not show a downshifting on SDS-PAGE.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Deacetylation of native acetylated RutR sparks autoproteolysis but denaturation inhibits this autoproteolytic activity.
source: These results are consistent with the possibility that deacetylation of native acetylated RutR sparks autoproteolysis but denaturation inhibits this autoproteolytic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the heat-denaturation experiments.

claim: K62Q, K62R, and the two double mutant RutR proteins showed diminished cleavage.
source: Measurement of the ratios of cleaved/intact RutR revealed that K52Q and K52R RutR behaved similar to WT RutR. In contrast, K62Q, K62R, and the two double mutant RutR proteins showed diminished cleavage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The apparent autoproteolytic activity of RutR is dependent on its deacetylation.
source: Therefore, we propose that the apparent autoproteolytic activity of RutR is dependent on its deacetylation and that removal of the acetyl group from K62 appears most important for its cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: Removal of the acetyl group from K62 appears most important for RutR cleavage.
source: Therefore, we propose that the apparent autoproteolytic activity of RutR is dependent on its deacetylation and that removal of the acetyl group from K62 appears most important for its cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing K62 mutants have diminished cleavage.

claim: The Km of YcgC is 2.13 ± 0.65 μM.
source: We thus performed steady-state assays to monitor the enzyme kinetics of YcgC via measuring the production of the downshifted RutR band, and estimated the Km and Vmax of YcgC to be 2.13 ± 0.65 μM and 0.29 ± 0.07 μM/min/μM, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on steady-state kinetic assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Vmax of YcgC is 0.29 ± 0.07 μM/min/μM.
source: We thus performed steady-state assays to monitor the enzyme kinetics of YcgC via measuring the production of the downshifted RutR band, and estimated the Km and Vmax of YcgC to be 2.13 ± 0.65 μM and 0.29 ± 0.07 μM/min/μM, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on steady-state kinetic assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: RutR was originally identified as a transcriptional repressor of the rutABCDEFG operon in E. coli.
source: Originally identified as a transcriptional repressor of the rutABCDEFG operon in E. coli, RutR (YcdC) was later found to bind to 19 additional E. coil chromosomal loci (Shimada et al., 2008), including the coding regions of pmrD and gcd (Umezawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RutR binds to 19 additional E. coli chromosomal loci.
source: Originally identified as a transcriptional repressor of the rutABCDEFG operon in E. coli, RutR (YcdC) was later found to bind to 19 additional E. coil chromosomal loci (Shimada et al., 2008), including the coding regions of pmrD and gcd (Umezawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RutR binds to the coding regions of pmrD and gcd.
source: Originally identified as a transcriptional repressor of the rutABCDEFG operon in E. coli, RutR (YcdC) was later found to bind to 19 additional E. coil chromosomal loci (Shimada et al., 2008), including the coding regions of pmrD and gcd (Umezawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of rutR alone does not result in significant elevation of expression levels of most of its target genes.
source: However, deletion of rutR alone does not result in a significant elevation of the expression levels of most of its target genes, suggesting that RutR regulates target gene transcription via a different mechanism.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge.

claim: RutR regulates target gene transcription via a different mechanism than simple repression.
source: However, deletion of rutR alone does not result in a significant elevation of the expression levels of most of its target genes, suggesting that RutR regulates target gene transcription via a different mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion doesn't increase target gene expression.

claim: Induction of ycgC did not change the expression level of rutR.
source: Interestingly, while induction of ycgC did not change the expression level of rutR, the expression of two rutR targeting genes, pmrD and gcd, was significantly decreased, by as much as fivefold as measured with quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) over a 2-hr period of ycgC induction (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Expression of pmrD and gcd was significantly decreased upon ycgC induction.
source: Interestingly, while induction of ycgC did not change the expression level of rutR, the expression of two rutR targeting genes, pmrD and gcd, was significantly decreased, by as much as fivefold as measured with quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) over a 2-hr period of ycgC induction (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Induction of cobB did not affect expression levels of rutR or any of the 15 RutR target genes.
source: On the other hand, induction of cobB in parallel did not affect expression levels of rutR or any of the 15 of RutR's target genes (data not shown), suggesting the possibility that YcgC regulates a different set of substrates from CobB.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: YcgC regulates a different set of substrates from CobB.
source: On the other hand, induction of cobB in parallel did not affect expression levels of rutR or any of the 15 of RutR's target genes (data not shown), suggesting the possibility that YcgC regulates a different set of substrates from CobB.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on gene expression.

claim: 197 genes were significantly repressed after 4 hr of ycgC induction.
source: Using a standard DNA microarray approach, we found that, compared with WT cells, 197 genes were significantly repressed and 93 genes were activated after 4 hr of ycgC induction.
evidence: This is based on DNA microarray data.

claim: 93 genes were activated after 4 hr of ycgC induction.
source: Using a standard DNA microarray approach, we found that, compared with WT cells, 197 genes were significantly repressed and 93 genes were activated after 4 hr of ycgC induction.
evidence: This is based on DNA microarray data.

claim: Expression levels of pmrD and gcd were significantly reduced after ycgC induction.
source: In agreement with the above observations, expression levels of pmrD and gcd were significantly reduced (Figure 4b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on DNA microarray data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: 4 hr of cobB induction resulted in 195 down-regulated genes and 136 up-regulated genes.
source: A similar analysis in parallel revealed that 4 hr of cobB induction resulted in 195 and 136 up- and down-regulated genes, respectively, compared with WT cells.
evidence: This is based on DNA microarray data.

claim: With the exception of xerC, none of RutR's targets was affected by cobB induction.
source: However, with the exception of xerC, none of the RutR's targets was affected (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on DNA microarray data.

claim: There is no significant overlap between up- or down-regulated gene groups in ycgC and cobB induction experiments.

claim: YcgC removes the acetyl groups on K52/62 of RutR via a Ser hydrolase activity.
source: In this study, we have applied a clip-chip approach to identify new KDAC candidates in E. coli. Our in-depth biochemical characterization revealed that the novel KDAC YcgC removes the acetyl groups on K52/62 of its substrates RutR via a previously unknown Ser hydrolyase activity.

claim: After deacetylated by either YcgC or CobB, RutR showed a significant downshift on SDS-PAGE.
